paragraphs: In early winter, the morning mist refused to lift from the Fei River. A salt boat lay at anchor midstream. Its bamboo shelter had been dismantled and fresh boards nailed along the gunwales, though old crystals of salt still clung to the seams. Two thick hawsers ran to the north and south banks, each held by soldiers of a different army. A little more force from either shore could turn this meeting into an abduction. Tiny bells hung at the rope ends, stirring faintly in the light wind.

Zhu Xu boarded first. He searched from the bilges to the roof beams, then had men from both armies bail the water out of the stern until the decking showed. Only after satisfying himself that no one hid beneath it did he send them away. Each army had withdrawn five hundred paces from the bank. Each delegation was limited to twelve people, and short knives were to remain sealed in their sheaths. Copies of the rules hung separately at bow and stern. The scribes had scarcely set down their brushes before damp air began to blur the ink.

Footsteps came first from the northern bank. Fu Jian wore a dark, close-fitting robe. Beneath his black cap, his white hair was startling. He put a hand on the rail as he climbed the gangway, then released it. Fu Rong followed without offering an arm. From the south, Liu Yu surrendered his sword and ducked beneath a slanting rope, mud from the embankment on his boots. He halted three paces from Fu Jian, and both men bowed. Zhu Xu, who had rehearsed two different sets of ceremonial introductions, spoke neither.

Only two low tables and two bowls of warm water had been provided. Everyone present was accustomed to magnificent ceremonies of alliance; such austerity felt strange. Fu Jian sat first and asked how many men Liu Yu had commanded when he rose at Jingkou. Liu Yu gave the true number, then reported how many new units he had raised in recent months, how many had died or been wounded, and how much grain was owed. At the mention of arrears, Fu Jian looked up. Liu Yu lifted his bowl, drank it empty, and set the earthenware down without a sound.
“If you mean to persuade me that the south can stand on its own,” Fu Jian said, “beginning with its grain arrears is an interesting choice.”
“Your Majesty has long known the south lacks grain,” Liu Yu replied. “That is why you brought an army here.”

Fu Jian signaled a clerk to produce the registers for the three cities. Baishi, Qinglin, and Shiliang each had Qin grain-allotment books, Qin household and guest-household registers, and garrison rosters. The Jin court’s reply lay beneath them. Two different governments had set their seals over the same household names, in varying shades of vermilion. Fu Jian turned one register toward Liu Yu. “Guo Cheng of Baishi’s northern ward received twelve mu of abandoned land last year. If you take the city, will you make him surrender it to the former Zhao owners?”
“He will cultivate it this winter as before,” Liu Yu said. “If the old owners bring a claim, each piece of evidence will be examined. That is how I handled such matters in Danyang.”
“Baishi’s county officials are not Jingkou’s. With your soldiers outside the walls, whose orders will they obey?”

Liu Yu drew out a household petition and set it beside the register. It came from a Baishi woman who had once hauled grain for the Qin army. Her husband wanted to retain his Qin registration; her son served in the Jin army. She sought no reward of grain. She asked to whom the ancestral fields could be sold if her husband moved north, and whether, if her son returned south, he would still be recognized as his father’s son.
“Neither county magistrate,” Liu Yu said, “has answered her.”

Fu Jian studied the thumbprint on the paper and told a Qin clerk to record the woman’s name. He asked Zhu Xu if he knew the family. Zhu Xu said he had seen the woman only once, at the ferry. She held her small grandson and waited until sunset, while no one could give her a written permit to pass. Fu Jian laid the petition beneath his own papers and did not return it.

Zhu Xu had brought two elders from Baishi. One carried a Qin grain voucher; the other an old Jin document. In their youth they had worked fields watered by the same canal. Now they stood among the northern and southern attendants respectively. The lee of the cabin was warmer, but even in the cold they refused to sit together. Liu Yu noticed and had them moved closer to the brazier. Both men rose to express their thanks, then sat again with half a foot of space between them.

Fu Rong spread out the garrison map. Water channels connected the three cities. Their inhabitants could use two gates, but troops could obey only one chain of command. If Jin forces took over, where were Qin troops to withdraw? If Qin troops remained, who would command the Jin court’s former officials? The attendants on both sides offered their answers, but stopped when they reached the granaries: the grain could be counted jointly, yet the keys could be handed to only one person.
“I came here thinking that, at the very least, I could spare these people a winter of fighting,” Fu Jian said.

Liu Yu glanced at the ledgers. “I will sign an agreement to let grain move freely through the ferry and forbid extortion by either army. As for command of the three cities, we can discuss it after the disputed land registers have been checked.”
“Checked until what year?”
“Until we can tell whose claims are valid.”
Fu Jian pointed to several altered names. “During the northern land surveys, some men used that very answer to conceal the truth for ten years.”

“But in the north,” Liu Yu said, “Your Majesty can arrest a magistrate and dismiss a great landowner. In a southern county, some old families are beyond even Jiankang’s reach. If Qin troops hold the city, who will dare testify on behalf of the Jin court?”

Neither answered immediately. Outside the cabin a boatman sounded the river with a pole. Bamboo struck the hull twice with a hollow knock. Fu Jian closed the register of Qin households and asked instead about Liu Yu’s recent orders against plunder. Seventeen, Liu Yu replied. Had plunder stopped everywhere in the south? Liu Yu shook his head. He had only just executed a commander at Jingkou who considered past service a license to do as he pleased; members of the man’s old unit were still protesting his innocence.
“Then you know,” Fu Jian said, “how far an edict still has to travel after it leaves Jiankang.”

“I do,” Liu Yu replied. “But I also know that wherever Your Majesty’s edict reaches, that place is counted as Qin territory. If the south hands over its military orders, granaries, and officials all at once, it will have to fight its way back to Chang’an should it ever wish to undo the decision.”

Fu Jian’s expression did not change. He told Fu Rong to hand over a draft compact: the Jin ancestral temples were to remain untouched; existing land deeds would be examined, not summarily voided; taxation was not to be abruptly altered for three years; southerners might continue to serve in county and commandery offices. Beifu officers and soldiers who chose Qin allegiance would retain their ranks; pay and rations would be entered in the Secretariat’s accounts. Two blank spaces remained at the end, left for Liu Yu’s proposed amendments.
Liu Yu read it and pushed it back. “This is more thorough than many an edict issued in the south.”
“And still unacceptable?”
“Once all this is written, who has the power to repeal it?”
“The Qin courts, Secretariat, and censors may all block or return an improper order.”
“And what can they not block?”

Fu Jian looked at the two spaces still blank on the document. The wooden time marker at the bow showed that more than half their allotted meeting had passed. Over many years he had tried to bind generals to military registers, compel royal kinsmen to relinquish private camps, and make counties verify household names before collecting grain. Yet he had also, in anger, dismissed his crown prince and forced his ministers to bow their heads. Asked about himself, he could find no answer without a flaw.
“The final authority still rests in my hands,” he said.
“Your Majesty admits as much,” Liu Yu answered. “That is more than those men at court in Jiankang would do. But the south cannot surrender its cities merely on the strength of that admission.”

Zhu Xu sensed their voices lowering and drew the attendants toward the bow. Fu Rong withdrew with them, never taking his eyes off Fu Jian. The wind suddenly set the mooring bells ringing. Boatmen hurried to shorten the northern cable; the salt boat swung slightly toward that bank, and Jin soldiers instantly tightened the opposite rope. Only when men on both sides saw that it was the river’s current, not a hostile move, did their fingers slowly loosen.
Looking at those two cables, Fu Jian suddenly asked, “You march beneath the Jin banner. Do you still revere the Sima house?”

Liu Yu did not evade him. “I revere the ancestral rites. That does not mean I revere whoever sits in their hall. When Huan Xuan entered Jiankang, had I not raised the Jin banner, the people of Jingkou would scarcely have known why I rebelled. But if the court still cannot govern in years to come, that banner may not protect them either.”
“You intend to replace the Jin house?”
“For now, I mean to keep the garrisons along the river secure and their soldiers' families fed. I will not deceive Your Majesty with an oath about what may come later.”

Fu Jian traced the rim of his bowl with a fingertip. How like his own voice, in his youth, when he had welcomed into Chang’an ministers of fallen kingdoms. He had believed then that with good generals and worthy advisers every fissure in the realm could be sewn shut, one after another. Wang Meng had written many memorials of remonstrance while he lived. Fu Jian had treasured them, sometimes smiling as he read. Since Wang’s death, however, he had often taken them out and sat over some unresolved affair of state until deep into the night.
“If Jinglüe could see you,” Fu Jian said, “I doubt he would like you.”
“Nor,” Liu Yu replied, “would he trust Your Majesty entirely.”
Fu Jian actually laughed. “No. He never trusted me entirely.”

After a while Liu Yu asked why, having already withdrawn his army over five days, Fu Jian had come in person to the Jiang–Huai region. Fu Jian said he had heard many accounts of the south in Chang’an: Xie An’s memorials, Zhu Xu’s old documents, and the depositions of refugees from the Huai. In his youth he had wanted only to cross one river. Now he had halted before it for twenty years, his hair entirely white. Crossing or not crossing could no longer be decided with a single military command.

“I want to see the realm united before I die,” he said, looking directly at Liu Yu. “I also want to know that the north will not rise in rebellion when I am gone, merely because it has lost one man. The two wishes may not be compatible.”

“I have seen what it costs the south to change its master,” Liu Yu said. “Huan Xuan replaced the Jin emperor’s seal, and the people of Jiangling collected grain for him. I restored the Jin seal, and those who were supposed to receive grain still went hungry. If we make them accept a Qin seal as well, who will shoulder the burden of feeding them?”
“Granaries, roads, and a corps of officials who must distribute grain even when the emperor changes. It has taken the north more than twenty years to build even a tolerable version of that.”
“The south needs years of its own to do the same.”
“I fear I do not have those years left.”

Liu Yu looked steadily at the old man. The lines of his face were deep, and his fingers trembled slightly in the cold wind. Yet the orders governing eighty thousand Qin troops on both banks still reached their units; the axles of grain wagons and the ledgers at tax barriers seemed connected to those aging hands. Every assertion Fu Jian made could be checked against an account. The more Liu Yu listened, the less willing he became to stake the whole south on what might be decided aboard this salt boat today.

“In Your Majesty’s early years, you wanted the Yan people to forget Yan and the Qiang to forget the Qiang,” Liu Yu said. “Murong Chui now holds an army for you. That is already a great distance to have traveled. But he has never forgotten Ye.”
Fu Jian looked up. “You know he is ill?”
“Every soldier along the river knows. In camps he once commanded, there are still men who remember old songs of Yan.”

Fu Jian said nothing. The north wind strengthened outside the cabin, bending the reeds along the shore almost into the water. Qin registers and Jin documents lay between the men; neither removed a single volume.

As their allotted time drew to a close, Zhu Xu returned to the cabin. Fu Jian asked whether, if Qin troops withdrew another fifty li northward, the Jin army could promise not to seize the three cities. Liu Yu replied that they could discuss a temporary cessation of hostilities and joint verification of households and fields, but the garrisons and the city gates must first be settled. Fu Jian would not abandon soldiers protecting households already registered under Qin; Liu Yu could not allow the Jin emperor’s orders to remain forever outside the walls. They looked at one another, and at last both rose.

Zhu Xu asked them to sign the two points already agreed: merchant vessels and physicians could pass according to their registers, and neither side might privately detain a person for an earlier household registration or for former service transporting grain; officials of both states would continue to examine the disputed claims to the three cities, while neither army might cross the marked lines of warning without authorization. All other conditions were entered as unresolved. Fu Rong read every word, and Liu Yu’s clerk checked every word again. When the two ink signatures were placed on the paper, there were no drums or ceremonial music.

Taking back his copy, Liu Yu said, “We did not settle the cities today. But at least the woman at the ferry, holding her grandson, need not wait tonight for another promise that exists only on paper.”
“A document must reach the county,” Fu Jian said, “and someone there must be willing to obey it. Both our armies should watch their own men.”

As they prepared to leave, both thick cables were released together. The big boat drifted with the current for a moment before the small escort craft from either bank approached. Fu Rong steadied Fu Jian by the arm, and this time his father did not push him away. Liu Yu stepped into his skiff and bowed once more across the water. Zhu Xu remained aboard until both escorts were clear, then handed the two earthenware bowls to a boatman to wash. One had an old hairline crack in its base; when warm water was poured into it, a slow leak began.

On the road to the northern camp, Fu Rong asked about preparations for war. Fu Jian ordered him to send both copies of the compact to Chang’an, together with the unresolved draft, for Fu Hong and the departments to preserve in their archives. Even if war came later, the provisions already accepted on passage and immunity were not to be swept aside by the advance of an army. Fu Rong agreed, then reported that Murong Chui had coughed blood that morning. The army physician was staying at his tent.
Fu Jian reined in his horse and did not move for a long time.

On the southern bank, Liu Yu too was studying the reports brought back to him. Jingkou had collected nearly a fifth less grain this year, and two military granaries were auditing old arrears. He Wuji urged him to strike while the Qin ruler was growing old. Liu Yu laid the military report beneath the ferry compact he had just signed.
“First let the grain boats that are allowed to cross go through,” he said. “Tonight, when our soldiers inspect the ferries, arrest the first man who dares extort so much as another dou of grain.”

Far away, Qin troops were changing the watch. Horn calls traveled along the northern shore, and after a little while drums answered from the south. Neither army broke camp. At midstream the salt boat’s new boards were taken off. Its owner arrived to reclaim it and asked whether he might still sail the old trade route. The boatmen told him that both states had given permission today. One slung a coil of rope over the owner’s shoulder and laughed: the two words “permission granted” were light enough on paper, but several checkpoints still stood between paper and the ferry. The owner merely weighed the rope in his hand and said nothing.
